code: bam_interpret(     x             = fit   , higher_better = TRUE   , top           = 5   ) Bayesian AMMI analysis  2 bilinear term(s): lambda_1 = 5,459, lambda_2 = 1,695; the chains have converged.  Findings: - The chains have converged by the criteria of Crossa et al. (2011) (largest   potential scale reduction factor 1.004); the smallest effective sample size   of the main parameters is 657. - 4 of 132 Heidelberger-Welch stationarity and half-width tests failed (about   5% fail by chance at level 0.05). - Overall mean 4,858 (95% HPD 4,796 to 4,920); error variance 762,200, a   coefficient of variation of 18.0%. - Genotypes significantly above average (HPD of the effect excludes zero): 4,   5 and 6; below average: 1, 2, 7 and 8. - Environments with significantly high means: 4, 6, 11, 12, 13 and 2 more;   low: 1, 2, 7, 8, 10 and 2 more. - Singular values with 95% HPD intervals: lambda_1 = 5,459 (4,527 to 6,306);   lambda_2 = 1,695 (59.23 to 2,892). - On the first bilinear term, genotypes with significantly positive scores:   4, 5, 6 and 9; negative: 1, 2, 3 and 8. - Environments with significantly positive first scores: 11, 12, 13, 15 and   18; negative: 1, 3, 8 and 10. - Genotypes and environments with significant first scores of the same sign   interact positively: the genotype yields more there than its main effect   predicts; of opposite sign, less.  Recommendations: - Recommend the genotypes with significant first scores for the environments   whose scores have the same sign (biplots() shows the regions). - Draw biplots() to see which genotypes and environments form homogeneous   groups (overlapping HPD regions). title: Interpreting the results
text: rules: Convergence: potential scale reduction factor 1.1, effective sample size main parameters least 400, Raftery-Lewis dependence factor 5, 10% Heidelberger-Welch tests failed. Main effects: genotype environment differs average HPD interval effect excludes zero. Bilinear terms: term whose HPD interval \(\lambda_k\) reaches tenth posterior mean weakly supported. Interaction: significant first scores sign mean positive interaction.
code: txt <-   bam_interpret(       x             = fit     , higher_better = TRUE     , top           = 5     ) txt Bayesian AMMI analysis  2 bilinear term(s): lambda_1 = 5,466, lambda_2 = 1,646; the chains have converged.  Findings: - The chains have converged by the criteria of Crossa et al. (2011) (largest   potential scale reduction factor 1.003); the smallest effective sample size   of the main parameters is 862. - 5 of 131 Heidelberger-Welch stationarity and half-width tests failed (about   5% fail by chance at level 0.05). - Overall mean 4,858 (95% HPD 4,793 to 4,920); error variance 763,800, a   coefficient of variation of 18.0%. - Genotypes significantly above average (HPD of the effect excludes zero): 4,   5 and 6; below average: 1, 2, 7 and 8. - Environments with significantly high means: 4, 6, 11, 12, 13 and 2 more;   low: 1, 2, 7, 8, 10 and 2 more. - Singular values with 95% HPD intervals: lambda_1 = 5,466 (4,538 to 6,343);   lambda_2 = 1,646 (15.93 to 2,835). - On the first bilinear term, genotypes with significantly positive scores:   4, 5, 6 and 9; negative: 1, 2, 3 and 8. - Environments with significantly positive first scores: 11, 12, 13, 15 and   18; negative: 1, 3, 8 and 10. - Genotypes and environments with significant first scores of the same sign   interact positively: the genotype yields more there than its main effect   predicts; of opposite sign, less.  Recommendations: - Recommend the genotypes with significant first scores for the environments   whose scores have the same sign (biplots() shows the regions). - Draw biplots() to see which genotypes and environments form homogeneous   groups (overlapping HPD regions).  Cautions: - The HPD interval of lambda_2 reaches down to near zero: the term is weakly   supported and its scores are uncertain.  Sources: - Crossa, J., Perez-Elizalde, S., Jarquin, D., Cotes, J. M., Viele, K., Liu,   G. and Cornelius, P. L. (2011). Bayesian estimation of the additive main   effects and multiplicative interaction model. Journal of the Royal   Statistical Society B, 64(4), 583-639. doi:10.1111/1467-9868.00353 - Watanabe, S. (2010). code: bp <-   biplots(       model         = fit     , burnin        = 0     , thin          = 0.5     , pb            = 0.05     , plot_stable   = TRUE     , plot_unstable = TRUE     , ncolors       = 5     , .which        = "both"     , .grid         = 100     ) bam_interpret(     x             = bp   , higher_better = TRUE   , top           = 5   ) Biplot with highest posterior density regions  7 of 9 genotypes and 8 of 20 environments have a 95% HPD region that excludes the origin (significant interaction).  Findings: - Genotypes whose region contains the origin (interaction not different from   zero, stable): 3 and 7. - Groups on the first term (marginal HPD interval excludes zero): positive 4,   5, 6 and 9; negative 1, 2, 3 and 8. - Environments on the first term: positive 4, 11, 12, 13, 15 and 1 more;   negative 1, 3, 8 and 10; the others do not differ from zero. - Overlapping regions mark genotypes (environments) whose interaction   parameters do not differ: a homogeneous group.  Recommendations: - Genotypes 4, 5, 6 and 9 are adapted to environments 4, 11, 12, 13, 15 and 1   more (both positive on the first term). - Genotypes 1, 2, 3 and 8 are adapted to environments 1, 3, 8 and 10 (both   negative on the first term).  Cautions: - The regions are estimated from the draws by a kernel density; with few   draws their outline is rough. - The second term is usually estimated with much more uncertainty than the   first: long regions along the second axis.  Sources: - Crossa, J., Perez-Elizalde, S., Jarquin, D., Cotes, J. M., Viele, K., Liu,   G. and Cornelius, P. L. (2011). text: Every interpretation ends sources method; bam_cite() gives BibTeX.
code: fs <-   bayes_stability(       .data   = Maiz     , .y      = y     , .gen    = entry     , .env    = site     , .rep    = rep     , .model  = "ER"     , .nIter  = 2000     , .burnin = 500     , .thin   = 1     , .chains = 2     , .priors = bam_stab_priors(           mu_var = NULL         , g_var  = NULL         , h_var  = NULL         , b_var  = 100         , nu     = 1         , s2     = NULL         , nu_d   = 1         , s2_d   = NULL         )     , .level  = 0.95     , .alpha  = 0.05     , .seed   = 8     , .waic   = TRUE     ) bam_interpret(     x             = fs   , higher_better = TRUE   , top           = 5   ) Bayesian Eberhart-Russell stability model  Best by the safety-first index (alpha = 0.05): 6, 5, 3, 9 and 4; most probably the best: 6 (0.84).  Findings: - The chains may not have converged (largest potential scale reduction factor   1.011; smallest effective sample size of the main parameters 383). - Slopes whose HPD interval lies above 1 (respond more than average to good   environments): 4 and 5; below 1 (respond less, relatively better in poor   environments): 8. - Smallest deviation variance: 6 (74,500); largest: 1 (502,000). - Share of each genotype's variation explained by the regression (R2): 1   0.73, 2 0.88, 3 0.93, 4 0.94, 5 0.95, 6 0.96, 7 0.86, 8 0.57, 9 0.94.  Recommendations: - For a wide recommendation choose genotypes with a high mean, a slope near 1   and a small deviation variance; for favourable environments a slope above 1   with a high mean. - The safety-first index combines the two: 6, 5 and 3 lead.  Cautions: - The chains have not converged by the criteria used; run longer chains   before using the estimates. - The environmental index is estimated from the same trial; with few   environments the slopes are uncertain (see the HPD intervals).  Sources: - Eberhart, S. A. and Russell, W. A. (1966). Stability parameters for   comparing varieties. Crop Science, 6(1), 36-40.   doi:10.2135/cropsci1966.0011183X000600010011x - Oliveira, T. R. code: cat(strwrap(x = txt$guide, width = 80), sep = "\n") Bayesian AMMI: every parameter has a posterior distribution, summarised by its mean, standard deviation and highest posterior density (HPD) interval. Main effects whose HPD interval excludes zero differ from the average. Singular values measure the strength of each bilinear term. Genotype and environment scores with HPD intervals excluding zero interact significantly; same signs mean positive interaction. Check convergence first: potential scale reduction factor near 1, large effective sample sizes, Raftery-Lewis dependence factor below 5, Heidelberger-Welch tests passed.

Every parameter posterior distribution, AMMI biplot gets statistical inference: highest posterior density (HPD) regions show genotypes environments interact significantly form homogeneous groups. bayes_ammi(): Gibbs sampler (overall mean, genotype environment effects, singular values, scores constrained spheres, error variance), several chains, burn-, thinning, priors bam_priors(), posterior summaries HPD intervals convergence diagnostics Raftery-Lewis, Heidelberger-Welch Gelman-Rubin; biplots(): biplot HPD regions genotype environment coordinates; ge_ammi(), ge_mean(), ge_eff() friends: least-squares AMMI tables built ; bam_interpret(): plain-language interpretation every result, computed numbers. Beyond article: unbalanced trials (missing plots empty cells, data augmentation) environment-specific error variances (.het = TRUE); Bayesian GGE (sites regression) model (.model = "GGE") bam_winners(), probability genotype wins environment; decisions breeders: bam_superiority() (probabilities superior performance stability Dias et al. 2022), bam_ranks(), bam_stability() (Bayesian AMMI stability value interaction variance) bam_predict() (every cell, observed ); Bayesian stability analysis: bayes_stability() fits Finlay-Wilkinson, Eberhart-Russell Shukla models Gibbs sampling (slopes, deviation stability variances, Eskridge’s safety-first index, HPD intervals); bam_indices() bam_ammi_indices() give posterior distributions Wricke’s, Shukla’s, Lin Binns’, Annicchiarico’s Eskridge’s indices ASV, SIPC, EV, Za, WAAS WAASY; model choice: DIC WAIC bam_compare(), posterior predictive checks bam_ppc(), draws posterior, bayesplot coda; bam_app(): application runs every analysis without code, results copy cleanly. Version 1.0.0 rewrites sampler version 0.3.0, , among faults, never updated singular values return error variance (see NEWS). new sampler runs C++ reproduces Tables 1 B1 Crossa et al. (2011). Every function keeps name, arguments result components; fifteen vignettes come HTML PDF. Every printed result ends sources method; bam_cite() gives BibTeX.
